newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa Reserve Bank not engineering weaker rand.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa Reserve Bank not engineering weaker rand.

text.p: The Reserve Bank had no determined policy to allow the South African rand to weaken in the wake of the plunge in the gold price, the central bank's deputy governor James Cross said on Wednesday.

Foreign exchange traders have speculated that the Reserve Bank had been buying dollars to engineer a weaker rand because of concerns about the effects the weaker gold price would have on its reserves and the country's export proceeds.
The rand has weakened three cents in the last three days to just under 4.56 against the dollar.
"There is no determined policy by the Reserve Bank to weaken the rand," Cross told Reuters in an interview.

"We are a constant buyer of any oversupply of dollars in the market against our forward book as people unwind their forward positions, but we have not been doing that to weaken the rand because of the weaker gold price," he said.
The gold price has fallen to its lowest level since 1985 in the wake of an announcement by the Reserve Bank of Australia that it sold 167 tonnes of the metal in the first half of this year.
It was fixed at a fresh 12-year low of $315.75 an ounce in London earlier.

Economists say the lower price will result in South Africa's gold reserves -- currently some 3.77 million ounces -- being devalued, while also reducing the country's export earnings of which gold makes up some 20 percent.
Of more concern was the threat to employment at marginal mines already struggling to manage soaring costs, they said.
Cross said that while there was reason to be concerned about the fall in the metal's price, it did not precipitate an immediate crisis.

"It does dent our terms of trade, but at the same time it is not the type of crisis it might have been 10 years ago," he said, noting that manufacturing exports in particular would offset losses from lower gold export proceeds.
Cross said the gold market currently appeared to be driven more by options hedging after the price fell through what many market participants had expected to be a floor at $330.
The Reserve Bank of Australia's announcement has led to speculation that more central bank selling could be expected as they shifted their focus away from gold.
Cross said the South African Reserve Bank had no plans to reduce its gold reserves -- currently in line with the world average of around 22 percent of total reserves.
"There is no plan by the bank to reduce its gold reserves. We have no need to," he said.
"They are falling as a proportion of total reserves and as a result we are moving into line with the rest of the world," he said.
